Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To find the image of a point under an affine transformation, all we need to do is substitute the position vector of the point into the formula for the affine transformation.

Content:

Content:
[MATH: [x; y]|= [1|1; − 1|1]_(⏟)_(A) ⋅ [u; v]_(⏟)_(u) + [− 1; 1]_(⏟)_(b).]

Content:

Content:

Content:
Therefore, the image of [MATH: P] is the point [MATH: P'({\color{black}-1},{\color{black}3})] in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Image of a Point or Segment

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
An affine transformation [MATH: \mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2] is a function of the form
[MATH: \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,]
where [MATH: \mathbf x, \mathbf u,] and [MATH: \mathbf b] are column vectors in [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] and [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

[MATH: [x; y]|= [u − v + 7; u + v + 1]; = [u − v; u + v] + [7; 1]; = [1|− 1; 1|1]_(⏟)_(A) ⋅ [u; v]_(⏟)_(u) + [7; 1]_(⏟)_(b).]

Therefore, the endpoints of the image in the [MATH: xy]-plane are [MATH: (0,-2)] and [MATH: (-3,1).]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Orientation-Preserving Transformations

Content:
An invertible affine transformation is orientation-preserving if it preserves the orientation of any polygon in the plane.

Content:
To understand this, let's go back to our triangle [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane and its image [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane under the action of the affine transformation [MATH: \mathbf T.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d6a074d4f649a5ab5a87e956fd0613db]

Content:
This transformation does not preserve orientation because when we traverse [MATH: \Delta] counterclockwise, its image [MATH: D] is traversed clockwise.

Content:
We can identify whether an affine transformation is orientation-preserving or not by examining the matrix [MATH: A] of the associated linear map. We have the following theorem:

Content:
> Suppose an affine transformation [MATH: \mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2] is defined as
> [MATH: \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,]
> where [MATH: \mathbf x, \mathbf u,] and [MATH: \mathbf b] are column vectors in [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] and [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix. Then, [MATH: \mathbf{T}] preserves orientation if
> [MATH: \det(A) > 0,]
> and does not preserve orientation if
> [MATH: \det(A) < 0.]

Item 13 — Tutorial: The Area Scale Factor of an Affine Transformation

Content:
Suppose an affine transformation [MATH: \mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2] is defined as
[MATH: \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,]
where [MATH: \mathbf x, \mathbf u,] and [MATH: \mathbf b] are column vectors in [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] and [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix.

Content:
Similar to the case of linear transformations, the area scale factor of [MATH: \mathbf T] is given by the determinant of [MATH: A.]

Content:
We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] by examining the area scale factor:

Content:
- If [MATH: |\det(A)|>1,] the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T] will have a larger area than [MATH: \mathcal P.]
- If [MATH: |\det(A)|=1,] the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T] will have the same area as [MATH: \mathcal P.]
- If [MATH: 0 < |\det(A)| < 1,] the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf T] will have a smaller area than [MATH: \mathcal P.]

Content:
Note that if [MATH: \det(A) = 0,] the image of [MATH: \mathcal P] is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

Content:
For example, consider the affine transformation [MATH: \mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,] from the previous discussion, defined as

Content:
[MATH: [x; y]|= [0|1; 1|0]_(⏟)_(A) ⋅ [u; v]_(⏟)_(u) + [1; − 1]_(⏟)_(b).]

Content:
Computing the determinant of [MATH: A,] we get
[MATH: 0|1; 1|0]

Content:
So, the area scale factor of the transformation is
[MATH: |\det(A)| = |-1| = 1.]

Content:
Thus, the area of triangle [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane and its image [MATH: D] under [MATH: \mathbf T] in the [MATH: xy]-plane have the same area.
